Title: Judge questions - a competent help needed!

Messages.Author: Ector
Messages.Body:
Here are some questions that I've got while being a judge for the last
year or more. Please assume that I'm not a novice CCG judge, as I was
a certified Magic judge (Level 2) prior to moving to VTES, and getting
such certificate isn't very simple.
Unfortunately, judging VTES tournaments proved to be much more
complicated than even judging a Magic Nationals. I'd like to get some
advices from the experienced judges, if possible.

Situation 1. Players A and C (grandprey of A) have a deal. Player B
declares an action to burn Army of Rats of player A. Playes C plays
Eagle's Sight and tries to block the action without even waiting for
player A's reaction. Player B plays superior Elder Impersonation, and
player C cannot block this action anymore. Then player A says that he
didn't refused to block yet, and asks whether he can attempt to block
now.

My response was: "Player C should wait until Player A refuses to block
the action, since A has the first priority to block. So C gets a
warning for illegal play, and A can attempt to block now".

After that the players argued that C could play Eagle's Sight since
the text reads "ignoring the normal prey, predator or target
restrictions for blocking actions". I'm pretty sure that my
interpretation of this was correct - it means only the right to block
actions that you cannot normally block (Direct actions against other
players and non-Direct actions performed crosstable), not the right to
ignore the normal order of blocking priority, but the confirmation
would be great.

Situation 2. A player was going to be ousted by Dragonbound at start
of his turn, and he couldn't avoid that. He used his master phase to
burn Tensions in the Ranks by discarding two master cards. After his
turn ended and he was ousted, his predator (controller of the burned
Tensions) recalled that his prey couldn't burn Tensions, since he
played Rotschreck before. Thus, he attempted to return Tensions back
to play.

My response was: "The turn is ended, the player is ousted, and we
cannot make a rollback now, so the Tension cannot be returned, even
though it was burned improperly". In Magic judges have clear
guidelines for such cases: a judge can make a rollback if he thinks
that the game state didn't changed much, but if the turn was ended,
it's strongly adviced to leave the game as is. Usually both players
get warnings in such cases for not being careful enough.

I completely understand that it's impossible to provide "the best"
answer in such situation, but I want to know your opinion
nevertheless. What would you do? Do you think that a judge could allow
the player to return Tensions in play, and why?

Situation 3. The round time is running out, but some players are
arguing with a judge about his ruling on some play situation. After
several minutes they demand to get some additional play time due to
the discussion!

What would you do in such situation? In Magic, this case could be
considered "Unsporting Conduct - Severe" with an automatic
disqualification at all Rules Enforcement Levels, or or at least
"Unsporting Conduct - Major" with a game loss at lower RELs.

-----------------
Can anybody provide me an advice on the tournament procedure after
issuing Game Loss or disqualification? How should I re-build the table
seating after that? For instance, with 12 players I have three tables
with 4 players each. What should I do after issuing a Game Loss in the
first round?
I guess I cannot just "oust" the player in that round, since it would
break a table balance, so that player should lose the next round,
right? Does it mean that the seating order will remain the same, and
some table would play with 3 players?

Disqualification seems rather harsh. Issuing a game loss is very
tricky.

If you want to remove someone from the game, or someone has to go, for
instance, there's a few options I think are good to follow.

First what you have to do is make an assessment of table balance.
Optimally you don't want to give an unfair disadvantage to anyone left
on the table. How to act should be dependent on that.

Usual options include just straight up removal from the game, his
predator doesn't get a VP and now predates on his previous prey. This
is the best option if there's no obvious discrepancy between strength
and chance of survival between these three players.

If the prey of the to be removed player is less strong than the to be
removed player, then the better option would be to "poolbag" this
player. His predator has to remove all the pool of his now defenseless
prey, who then is ousted, granting the predator 6 pool and a VP.
This is also a popular option, but comes with a disadvantage, since
when the predating deck is a votedeck, he will be able to direct
damage onto his "next prey" without being blockable by said prey. (ie.
he chooses not to damage his current poolbag prey, but instead his
grandprey, who cannot defend, and he's certain of the VP provided by
said poolbag anyway.)
So with vote decks around you have to watch this option.

There's lots of other viable options, but these are the most popular
and easy.

Cheers,
B

> Situation 1. Players A and C (grandprey of A) have a deal. Player B

This is correct, as others have already stated; Eagle's Sight doesn't
override the timing. Player A possibly deserves a verbal warning for
sitting there and letting it all happen, but that depends on how it went
down; if player C really did jump the gun very fast, then it's
reasonable to expect that player A would just sit and let everything
handle itself first.

Also, I would rewind; put the Eagle's Sight and Elder Impersonation back
in each player's hands, and start from the beginning: allow player A to
decide whether or not he wants to block.

> Situation 2. A player was going to be ousted by Dragonbound at start
> of his turn, and he couldn't avoid that. He used his master phase to
> burn Tensions in the Ranks by discarding two master cards. After his
> turn ended and he was ousted, his predator (controller of the burned
> Tensions) recalled that his prey couldn't burn Tensions, since he
> played Rotschreck before. Thus, he attempted to return Tensions back
> to play.

Since the existence or nonexistence of Tension in the Ranks couldn't
have affected the overall table state during that player's turn, I would
return Tension to play and say "good point, you can't do that". If the
cards drawn as a result of burning Tension had affected gameplay
somehow, I'd try to reverse that as well; without further information I
can't tell for sure. However, I would definitely lean towards restoring
Tension in the Ranks to the table, no matter what.

> My response was: "The turn is ended, the player is ousted, and we
> cannot make a rollback now, so the Tension cannot be returned, even
> though it was burned improperly".

This is an awful ruling. Just because the turn has ended doesn't mean
that it's impossible to figure out what the game state should be.

> Situation 3. The round time is running out, but some players are
> arguing with a judge about his ruling on some play situation. After
> several minutes they demand to get some additional play time due to
> the discussion!

First mistake: Why are you arguing with players?

Never let a situation get out of control like this. You are the judge;
you have the authority. Each side should get an opportunity to state
their case; once the judge is satisfied that he has an accurate report
of the circumstances, a ruling is made. Excessive player whining
afterwards gets verbal warnings for starters and can continue on as
necessary until players quit whining or are, in the extreme, removed
from the building.

Sure, you could be wrong, but at the table is not the place to make that
decision, nor is it the right time to allow an argument that further
disrupts game play. You're the judge; use your judgement.

If the judge required several minutes to explain the ruling properly so
that all players understood, or if each side stating their case took
some time, then it would be quite appropriate to add, say, five or ten
minutes to the play clock for that table. The judging process should
not interfere with the normal flow of the game if at all possible.

> -----------------
> Can anybody provide me an advice on the tournament procedure after
> issuing Game Loss or disqualification? How should I re-build the table
> seating after that? For instance, with 12 players I have three tables
> with 4 players each. What should I do after issuing a Game Loss in the
> first round?

We need more information here about the circumstances. A Game Loss is
something you should avoid issuing at all costs _if possible_.

> I guess I cannot just "oust" the player in that round, since it would
> break a table balance, so that player should lose the next round,

Absolutely not. A Game Loss in the first round should apply only to
that round, not the next. If the game is in progress, you resolve the
Game Loss for _that_ table, at _that_ time. This can be either by
awarding the predator an oust and 6 pool, by turning the Lost player
into a poolbag (no actions, no minions, no blocks, but the predator must
bleed through the remaining pool), or by any of a number of suggested
resolutions in other threads. But you should never penalize a player's
future rounds unless you are disqualifying them from the tournament flat
out.

- --
Derek

You start with "A and C have a deal". Either that is irrelevant to the timing of
the block, or it means that A and C are agreed that C will block (and therefore
A will implicitly decline to block). If the latter, then the proper ruling is to
play on. It's up to the judge to decide which is the case, of course.

Assuming the judge determines that the deal is irrelevant to the case at hand,
then it's all up in the air, just waiting for the judge to figure out what has
transpired implicitly and what has been skipped.

If player A didn't realize the timing rules for blocking (unlikely), then rewind.

If player A would have been agreeable to C's offer of "don't bother blocking
this one; I'll Eagle's Sight it", then play on (with A's implicit " no block"
now part of the explicit landscape. This is likely close to reality given the "A
and C have a deal" preface.

For the cases in between, rewinding is possible, but the exposing of B's Elder
Impersonation is game-altering enough to classify as an advantage to either A or
C or both. There are several ways to remedy this (restoring the game balance, if
not the exact state), depending on how much of an advantage it is (and how much
complicity from A and B was involved in C's misplay:

1. Rewind, but shuffle C's Eagle Sight into his deck (or into his top X cards)
and have him draw back up. Rewind back to B's announcement of "burn Army" (since
B's hand hasn't changed).

2. In conjunction with 1 above, shuffle B's Elder Impersonation in his deck (or
into the top Y cards) and have him draw back up. If this is done, rewind to
before the start of the action (and B can choose any action, based on his new hand).

3. In conjunction with 1 or 1 and 2 above, untap B's acting minion if the action
to block the Army is blocked. (Unlikely, but just illustrating the leeway the
judge has in rebalancing the table).

In all, "play on" seems to be the most likely scenario from the data given (that
is, A's acceptance of deal-mate C's Eagle's Sight block attempt without an
interruption of "wait C, I get to try to block first" indicates that he is
satisfied with passing his block attempts and letting C attempt to block).

> Situation 2. A player was going to be ousted by Dragonbound at start
> of his turn, and he couldn't avoid that. He used his master phase to
> burn Tensions in the Ranks by discarding two master cards. After his
> turn ended and he was ousted, his predator (controller of the burned
> Tensions) recalled that his prey couldn't burn Tensions, since he
> played Rotschreck before. Thus, he attempted to return Tensions back
> to play.
>
> My response was: "The turn is ended, the player is ousted, and we
> cannot make a rollback now, so the Tension cannot be returned, even
> though it was burned improperly". In Magic judges have clear
> guidelines for such cases: a judge can make a rollback if he thinks
> that the game state didn't changed much, but if the turn was ended,
> it's strongly adviced to leave the game as is. Usually both players
> get warnings in such cases for not being careful enough.
>
> I completely understand that it's impossible to provide "the best"
> answer in such situation, but I want to know your opinion
> nevertheless. What would you do? Do you think that a judge could allow
> the player to return Tensions in play, and why?

Since Tension could not have been removed, it stays.

Leaving it in play doesn't change the balance of the table from what it would
have been if the illegal activity had not occurred. Removing it does change the
balance of the table (most likely, unless it Tension is completely irrelevant,
in which case leaving it in play also won't matter).

> Situation 3. The round time is running out, but some players are
> arguing with a judge about his ruling on some play situation. After
> several minutes they demand to get some additional play time due to
> the discussion!
>
> What would you do in such situation? In Magic, this case could be
> considered "Unsporting Conduct - Severe" with an automatic
> disqualification at all Rules Enforcement Levels, or or at least
> "Unsporting Conduct - Major" with a game loss at lower RELs.

Add time, if the judge feels like it (the players "ask", they can never "demand").

The judge can always add time to restore the time spent making a ruling, if he
feels it is warranted. In the case of the impending timing limit, it seems
warranted.

> -----------------
> Can anybody provide me an advice on the tournament procedure after
> issuing Game Loss or disqualification? How should I re-build the table
> seating after that? For instance, with 12 players I have three tables
> with 4 players each. What should I do after issuing a Game Loss in the
> first round?
> I guess I cannot just "oust" the player in that round, since it would
> break a table balance, so that player should lose the next round,
> right? Does it mean that the seating order will remain the same, and
> some table would play with 3 players?

Mid-game game loss is handling in-table only (not by reseating). By ousting if
balance allows that (i.e., if he's about to be ousted already). But usually by
removing him and restoring the game balance (e.g., with awards of full or
fractional VPs, awards of 0-6 pool, tapping or untapping of minions or other
cards, movement of blood/life to or from minions, and so on). Ideally, a judge
will simply step in to play the remainder of the ejected player's game (with the
ejected player's cards, adjusted as necessary to correct deck discrepancies, if
any).

If disqualification leaves the tourney with an unsanctionable number, then the
tournament becomes unsanctioned (and the judge can proceed in any manner he
likes -- rearranging as he likes).

To avoid becoming unsanctioned, the judge can play (and use the multi-judge
rules) if he was not playing already (and can find suitable assitant
judge/players), or he can recuse himself if he was playing in a multi-judge event.

Actually, my Magic experience helped me a lot (not in these
situations, though). Magic judges also have to use their own judgement
in many cases. For instance, the judge doesn't have to assemble a
court to accuse somebody in cheating - if he believes in cheating,
that's enough. In both games, the "Unsportsmanlike conduct"
definitions and penalties are almost the same. Any experienced Magic
judge knows "by heart" when he has to intervene, and when he should
not, what penalty he should issue and why, and so on. In the
"uncivilized" countries like Belarus the judge is also a teacher, so
he should know all his players very well to encourage them for playing
better, not to discourage them. In both games any judge ruling should
not provide any advantages for some players, and so on. As you can
easily guess, I'm quite experienced in all these matters.
No game has a textbook with EVERY single answer. Still, Magic judges
have much more detailed recommendations than VTES judges. For
instance, they have a clear recommendation for rollbacks: "You can
rollback if not much happened since the mistake, but no rollbacks
after the turn ends". I don't have such clear recommendation in VTES,
though I'd like to. Things like returning the improperly destroyed
permanent to the game without actually rolling the game back never
happen in Magic, and I was quite surprised to know that they are
recommended here. I know that I will have to use my own judgement in
such cases, and I will try to "repair" the game as I can, having in
mind that the player who made the mistake deserves some "punishment"
during the "repair". For instance, in the mentioned illegal Fame
example I'm going to return all burned pool (and blood of the Famed
vampire), return the vampire to the Ready region and move Fame to the
owner's ash heap as a "punishment". What can you say about such
ruling?

judges have a regular "Rules Questions" column, a separate forum for

open for all discussions, and filtering the rules questions isn't
easy. I'd also would be happy to get an official document like
Comprehensive Rules, describing all "windows to play" and examples of
the most complicated situations. And my players would be happy to get
such document, too.

If you are allowing players to argue with you to the point that you're
considering issuing Unsportsmanlike Conduct warnings to them, I would
suggest that you need *vast* amounts more experience at judging before
you can claim it's helping you any.

Telling a player: "That's my ruling. Sit down. Play." is a
fundamental, necessary ability that you should have picked up within the
first couple of tournaments you judged of *any* game.

>No game has a textbook with EVERY single answer. Still, Magic judges
>have much more detailed recommendations than VTES judges. For
>instance, they have a clear recommendation for rollbacks: "You can
>rollback if not much happened since the mistake, but no rollbacks
>after the turn ends".

V:TES has pretty clear recommendations on this too.

- Rollback if you can.
- Correct state if you can't.
- Make corrections to game state as appropriate if it comes to light
later on. (That is, bodge as best as you can, if you feel it's
still necessary.)

Note that Magic can more often be rolled back in some situations where
V:TES can't easily be rolled back, because of V:TES's dynamic draw
mechanism. It might only be two or three actions into the turn of a
player with a lot of minions/actions, but far too much may have happened
for a judge to be confident to roll back. Each card played will be
redrawn. In Magic - typically - there are far fewer cards being drawn
than in the most prolific V:TES scenarios where a dozen or more cards
can fly on a single action.

A hard and fast rule like "roll back to the start of the turn" would
miss the simplicity of rolling back several turns at e.g. the start of
the game (say, I Sudden your Dreams of the Sphinx, and then play my own
Info Highway, and a couple of turns pass before anyone has brought
anything out - roll-back is easy!), and miss the complexities

> For instance, in the mentioned illegal Fame
>example I'm going to return all burned pool (and blood of the Famed
>vampire), return the vampire to the Ready region and move Fame to the
>owner's ash heap as a "punishment". What can you say about such
>ruling?

Without more details of the situation, it is hard to say.

However, in general, punishments should be applied to the player.
Corrections should be made to the game state based on how to best
correct it, rather than who to punish.

The end result *may* be the same, but the motivation for correcting the
game state is one of restoring what would/should have happened. Which
you can't do perfectly, most of the time.

>> If you want a little textbook of V:TES judging, you're not going to get
>> one.
>I'd like to have a separate newsgroup for the judges, at least.

You wouldn't get the votes for it.[0] Nor would it be helpful. Every
player may be a judge, particularly in multi-judge situations.

Additionally, it will inevitably transpire that many judging queries
stem from a mis-understanding of the game rules or card text. Players
don't need Yet Another Forum to follow for card text rulings! That
makes the player's life harder.

And judge and tournament questions would still turn up in every other
V:TES forum (web, newsgroups, mailing lists etc.), because of players
who don't know about, don't want to use, or can't use the dedicated
forum.

>Magic judges have a regular "Rules Questions" column, a separate forum
>for rules questions ONLY, and a special mailing list. This newsgroup is
>open for all discussions, and filtering the rules questions isn't easy.

There are several quick ways of doing this.

1) Use a real news-reader (i.e. not Google Groups). Most of these will
let you filter posts by specific people, or search for posts by
specific people. (A popular recommendation used to be Free
Agent.) If you're in a hurry, a search for unread posts by LSJ
will bounce you through most of the important rulings based
threads. If you find any that are interesting (i.e. not just
simple one line rulings) or any threads that suddenly exploded
into 100 posts, it might be worth looking in. However, it's
extremely rare to find a substantive thread on tournament policy
and judging that doesn't have a post from LSJ in it. (Even if
it's just a "Correct" to some other player's interpretation of
the situation.)

1a) If necessary, do an Advanced Search using the Google Groups
interface and replicate the above. It's less fun, but posts by
LSJ in the last month (or whatever period of time you've been
busy) will do much the same, just be less fun.

2) Encourage the use of a descriptive tag in headers. Many decks are
identified by "Deck:" or "[DECK]" or something. Ditto, TWDA
entries. Questions to LSJ often get "LSJ" in the Subject. Just
start using a "Judge:" tag in your headers. (I'd suggest not
using square brackets [ ] because Google has a tendency to eat
them.) If it's useful, it'll catch on.

> I'd also would be happy to get an official document like
>Comprehensive Rules, describing all "windows to play" and examples of
>the most complicated situations. And my players would be happy to get
>such document, too.

If you want one, write one. And ask for input. And actually do
something with that input. Then re-draft it. Repeat. With a careful
hand, this doesn't actually need that much work on your part; if you get
two or three players discussing a given point, they may thrash out text
for you.

Many years ago, LSJ used to maintain such documents that were quite
comprehensive at the time. (V:TES has moved on quite way since then.)
This would serve as a useful model for your attempts, as well as showing
the difficulties that such a document will have so you can avoid some of
them.

[0] Go read up on how to create Usenet newsgroups in the rec.*
hierarchy. You'd need something like 130 people in favour to even think
about creating it. Many more if there's even a whiff of drafting in
uninterested friends to vote for it.

The only transferable skills that exist between judging V:TES and M:TG
are the same that you would find judging and refereeing any game or
sport that the players take remotely seriously. Carry yourself in a
manner that commands respect and have the ability to back up your
assertions.

Anything else is pointless. Stating you have a professional soccer
refereeing qualification would carry more weight. Stating you have
M:TG level 2 means you are capable of running off and getting the
Level 4/5 judge to come and deal with a whinging teenager at a Pro
Tour who disagrees with your ruling, be it correct or not, and that
you are capable of counter-signing a results slip.

Passing a judging exam doesn't necessarily equate to you automatically
becoming a good and competant judge. Take two early Magic judges as
examples: Beth Morisund (Level 4) was fabulous at rules comprehension
and the intricacies of the game. She was not good at face to face
confrontation though. Tom Wylie (Level 4) alledgedly assaulted a
player.

Given a choice I would prefer a judge with good interpersonal skills
over rules knowledge.

Oh, of course it does. Where it DOESN'T work is if you show favoritism,

entirely on card text and your knowledge of the rules and procedures.

> A judge has to make the right decisions, or else there will be bad

If a judge makes a ruling based on card text, the rules, and tournament
procedures, and gets it wrong, there may be some disappointment, but why
will there be bad feelings?

If some of your players tend to harbor "bad feelings" when a judge has
ruled against them, I would think those would show up regardless of the
correctness of the ruling at issue. At this point, the problem is with
the player, not with the judge or style of judging.

I can assure you of this; sitting and allowing players to argue with you
_always_ causes bad feelings, especially if you change your ruling as a
result of the argument. For one, most of the time you'll be changing it
to something "wrong", or in the best case, something no more "right"
than your original ruling. And two, you have guaranteed that all of
your rulings are now subject to debate and vote at the time of the
ruling -- because you just taught the person who was ruled against that
if he doesn't like what you said, he just has to convince you and you'll
change it.

This is awful for a playgroup. I don't recommend it.

Since no one else has put it up yet, I will. From the Judge's Guide:

"200. Correction of Game State
This section generally deals with returning the game to a fair and playable
state after certain types of infractions. Only the judge may make
corrections to the game state. Correction of the game state is done in
addition to and not instead of the application of the appropriate penalty
for the infraction.

Philosophy:

It is important that the player committing the infraction receive no
benefit in the game for doing so. If no significant game actions have taken
place, play should be backed-up to the point of the error. The error should
then be corrected and the game should proceed forward from that point. If
significant game actions have taken place (***such as moving to the next
player's turn*** or knowledge of another player's cards), the judge may
choose to leave the game undisturbed or may adjust the game state in some
other way (for instance, altering pool or blood levels) since players have
made play decisions based on the subsequent state of the game."

*** emphasis mine. Maybe Ector glanced over this, and thought it read the
same as M:tG's guidelines? It isn't, the section goes on to describe ways
in which acceptable alterations can occur _without_ rewinding everything
done in the turn.
But perhaps it may be made more clear that a change of player turn
doesn't itself mean that significant alteration of the game state has also
occured. Ector's example of realizing an illegally-burnt Tension just
after a player is ousted is a good example of a turn change with a
corresponding lack of significant changes to the game state, easily
correctable.

>> I know that I will have to use my own judgement in
>> such cases, and I will try to "repair" the game as I can, having in
>> mind that the player who made the mistake deserves some "punishment"
>> during the "repair". For instance, in the mentioned illegal Fame
>> example I'm going to return all burned pool (and blood of the Famed
>> vampire), return the vampire to the Ready region and move Fame to the
>> owner's ash heap as a "punishment". What can you say about such
>> ruling?
>
> Restoring game state balance isn't about punishment. It's about
> balance. Including punishment in there is at odds with balance. When
> 100% balance is not possible, then you should err on the side of
> punishment, but that's not the same as imposing punitive damages.
>

Right. As the Judge's Guide says, restoration of game state is done in
addition to, not as a substitute for the appropriate penalty (verbal,
warning, game loss, disqual.). I don't believe that restoring the game
state in a way that also penalizes the offender can be seen as reasonable
by any sort of read of 200. You try to fix the game state in a way that is
fair (returning illegally burned resources strikes me as fair) and offers
no advantage to any player. Punishing someone through alteration of the
game state to their disadvantage is not the stated goal here.

Regards
DaveZ

The PotNosVote decks? I think we have worked that one to death.

The VTES for money angle. Here's my take on it:

I think that if VTES were played for serious money, it would be a much
different game. Having observed the cutthroat/nasty nature of many
Magic and Vs. "Pro" players, I don't think I would like to play with
people like that. I find the cutthroat VTES player is much more jocular
in general.

Here's the thing: VTES is a game that requires being cutthroat, much
like the boardgame Diplomacy. It's sort of like playing someone you
can't be normally - but after the game you revert back to your nice
self. One reason it works is because there aren't any real stakes.
When you are cutthroat in VTES, it's all in the name of fun, or at the
most a box of boosters, even the continental championships. It's for
fun, it's not personal. You can be a dick, but in the end it doesn't
matter - you're friends with the guy afterward (usually). I may be
naive, but that's how I feel.

If the game was played for money, then that cutthroat nature becomes
more "real", i.e. you are now actually being a dick, because you are
taking something tangible, something quantifiable from your opponent -
the prize cash.

For me, I think that's the difference and why the game would change for
me if it was played for money. In addition, I think it might bring in
the cutthroat/nasty players, and many of the jocular types would leave.
That would also make the game less fun for me.

In addition, I think the rules would have to be fundamentally changed to
truly address collusion. As the rules stand right now, I don't think
collusion can be prevented, and if there was real money on the table,
collusion would be rampant. My suggestion is to embrace the collusion
by making Money VTES a game with 4-player tables and teams of 2. No
doubt others have other solutions. One solution that I am pretty sure
won't work is having judges try to prevent it. But now we are heading
down the road often traveled previously of trying to prevent collusion
and how to determine PTW.

Finally for me, I already spend too much time on this game, even for a
hobby. What if I decided to try Money VTES. And contrary to my
expectations, I really liked it? And I got even *more* serious about
it? I'd have to wait until they actually had a 12-step program to get
off Money VTES... The prospect is scary.
